newsitem.title: USA: Brazil imports sink U.S. soybean prices -- for now.
newsitem.headline: Brazil imports sink U.S. soybean prices -- for now.

text.p: Confirmation that U.S. soy processors are turning to Brazil to buy soybeans prompted a sharp selloff in Chicago futures on Wednesday but the imports are unlikely to have a long-term price impact, analysts said.

"It's going to be negative for the cash market for a while because it takes away some premium," said Dale Durchholz, grain analyst with Agrivisor Services in Bloomington, Ill. "But total world consumption is still strong."
Citing tight U.S. soybean supplies, Cargill Inc issued a statement during the trading session that it had contracted to purchase an unspecified quantity of Brazilian soybeans.
U.S. soybean stocks are at the lowest levels in 20 years and prices this spring have climbed to levels not seen since a Midwestern drought in 1988.
"To carry us through this period, Cargill and other companies have turned to the global market for additional supplies," the company said in its statement.
Earlier this year, Owensboro Grain, a small crusher in Kentucky, bought several cargos of soybeans from Brazil.

July soybeans at the Chicago Board of Trade closed down the 30-cent-per-bushel daily limit on the news at $8.30. The price was down from a high of $8.86 last Friday before rumors of the soybean imports began to circulate in the market.
Cargill said it would use the soybeans to supply its plants in the U.S. Southeast, which provide soymeal and other feeds to livestock and poultry producers.

On Wednesday, the Brazilian processor Ceval Alimentos said it was negotiating a sale of 40,000 tonnes of soymeal for shipment to the United States. Traders said the buyer was likely a large pork producer on the East Coast.
That news helped to send CBOT July soymeal down the $10 a ton daily limit to close at $273.10 a ton.
There were market rumors of other U.S. firms doing business in South America but confirmation of additional buys could not be immediately obtained.

Durchholz said news of Brazilian soy imports should not come as a surprise because U.S. commercial firms began to look at Brazil as a cheaper source of soybeans as soon as that country began actively harvesting in March.
Despite the sharp drop in Chicago prices Wednesday, the market is supported long term by strong world demand, he said.
"The fact is, that exports are still okay for this time of year. We're crushing more than we did recently and the overall off-take in the world is still quite good," Durchholz said.
But grain imports into the U.S., the top grain exporter, remain a touchy issue with U.S. farmers, since they support competing overseas farmers and pressure U.S. farm gate prices.

In January 1985, Cargill shocked U.S. farm circles by announcing a plan to import 25,000 tonnes of Argentine wheat to millers on the U.S. Gulf Coast. The plan was later withdrawn but it prompted U.S. Senate hearings to discuss the competitiveness of U.S. grain at the time.
"You'll hear some grumbling and you'll hear it talked about around the coffee table," Durchholz said. "But it's all about making money and they (farmers) understand that."
Traders said the psychological impact of Brazilian imports this year was muted by the switch to a more market-based farm economy in the U.S. and by historically low stocks.
Huge imports also aren't expected because shipping soybeans from Brazil only works out financially for soybean processors that have plants located near major U.S. ports, analysts said.
